Name the four spheres of the earth.
questions.a: Lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living world).

questions.q: How do the spheres interact?
questions.a: Water evaporates to air, rain erodes rocks, plants draw water and air - matter and energy cycle among all spheres.

questions.q: Why is earth called a connected system?
questions.a: A change in one sphere - say extra CO2 in air - affects water, land and life too.

questions.q: Name the layers of the atmosphere from the ground up.
questions.a: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

questions.q: In which layer does weather occur?
questions.a: The troposphere - the lowest layer holding most air and water vapour.

questions.q: What important gas concentrates in the stratosphere?
questions.a: Ozone, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.

questions.q: What causes a sea breeze during the day?
questions.a: Land heats faster than water; warm air over land rises and cooler sea air flows in to replace it.

questions.q: What is a land breeze at night?
questions.a: Land cools faster, so warm air over the sea rises and air flows from land to sea.

questions.q: How do valley and mountain breezes form?
questions.a: Slopes heat or cool faster than valley floors, driving upslope breezes by day and downslope ones at night.

questions.q: What are planetary winds?
questions.a: Steady large-scale winds (trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies) blowing from high to low pressure belts.

questions.q: Why do winds deflect to the right in the northern hemisphere?
questions.a: The earth's rotation (Coriolis effect) deflects moving air sideways.

questions.q: How do trade winds get their name?
questions.a: They blew steadily, helping sailing trade ships cross the oceans.

concepts.title: Ocean Currents and Global Heat Transport

questions.q: What drives ocean currents?
questions.a: Winds push surface water; differences in water temperature and density also drive large-scale currents.

questions.q: Give an example of a warm and a cold ocean current.
questions.a: Warm: Gulf Stream; cold: Labrador (or Humboldt) current.

questions.q: How do ocean currents affect climate?
questions.a: Warm currents warm coastal lands (western Europe) while cold currents cool and dry nearby coasts.

questions.q: What is the carbon cycle?
questions.a: The cycling of carbon among air, living things, oceans and rocks through photosynthesis, respiration, decay and combustion.

questions.q: Name two processes that put carbon dioxide into the air.
questions.a: Respiration and burning of fuels (also decay).

questions.q: How do fossil fuels fit into the carbon cycle?
questions.a: They are buried carbon of ancient plants; burning them releases that stored carbon back to the air quickly.

questions.q: What is the nitrogen cycle?
questions.a: The cycling of nitrogen between air, soil and living things through fixation, nitrification and denitrification.

questions.q: How does atmospheric nitrogen become usable by plants?
questions.a: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (and lightning) convert N2 into nitrates that roots absorb.

questions.q: What do denitrifying bacteria do?
questions.a: They convert soil nitrates back into nitrogen gas, returning it to the air.

questions.q: What is eutrophication?
questions.a: Over-enrichment of water with nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) causing algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill aquatic life.

questions.q: How do fertilisers cause eutrophication?
questions.a: Excess fertiliser washes into ponds and rivers, feeding algae which multiply and then decay, using up dissolved oxygen.

questions.q: Name one consequence of eutrophication in a lake.
questions.a: Fish die-offs from oxygen starvation (the water turns foul and algal scum covers the surface).
